articles.title: How to Choose the Right AI Chatbot for Research, Coding, and Content Creation
articles.excerpt: AI chatbots have become useful tools for developers, researchers, marketers, and content creators. From explaining complex concepts and debugging code to researching unfamiliar topics and drafting art…
articles.body: AI chatbots have become useful tools for developers, researchers, marketers, and content creators. From explaining complex concepts and debugging code to researching unfamiliar topics and drafting articles, AI assistants can help simplify everyday tasks. However, choosing the right AI chatbot isn't as simple as picking the most popular one. Different tools offer different capabilities, integrations, workflows, and ways to access information. Some users need an assistant that can research topics using web sources. Others want help writing cleaner code, analyzing documents, brainstorming ideas, or creating content more efficiently. The best choice depends on what you want to accomplish, how you work, and how carefully you need to verify the results.
articles.author: Bhavesh Patel

articles.title: Remote Unlock Is Three Links, Not One: Why a Smart Lock Fails at the Front Door
articles.excerpt: The short answer: pressing "unlock" in an app does not talk to your lock. It talks to a server, the server talks to a bridge, and the bridge talks to a lock that spends most of its life asleep. Three…
articles.body: The short answer: pressing "unlock" in an app does not talk to your lock. It talks to a server, the server talks to a bridge, and the bridge talks to a lock that spends most of its life asleep. Three hops, three different radios, three different failure modes. Almost every "my smart lock stopped responding" complaint is one of those hops, and people keep fixing the wrong one by buying a better Wi-Fi router. The three hops Hop one is your phone to the vendor cloud. This is the hop people actually test, because it is the only one with a visible spinner in the app. If your phone has mobile data, this hop is almost never the problem. Hop two is the cloud to something inside your house.

articles.title: I got tired of tutorials that hide the bill
articles.excerpt: Hello. I am Marc, and I write runcheap.dev — a small blog of executable technical guides. Not "executable" as in "here is a snippet". As in: the commands, the config file, the deploy, and the monthly…
articles.body: Hello. I am Marc, and I write runcheap.dev — a small blog of executable technical guides. Not "executable" as in "here is a snippet". As in: the commands, the config file, the deploy, and the monthly invoice at the end. I started writing it because I kept landing on tutorials that got me to a working app and then said "hosting starts at $4/month" and stopped. Four dollars for what, exactly? How much RAM? Is the backup included? Does it survive a database that does not fit in memory? So the rule on my blog is simple: every price carries the date I read it on the provider's own page , and every command was run somewhere before it was published. No affiliate links, no "as low as", no number I could not verify myself.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Exorcist is a dependency health scanner for package.json — the checks npm audit doesn't run. Drop in a…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Exorcist is a dependency health scanner for package.json — the checks npm audit doesn't run. Drop in a file (or paste a GitHub repo URL) and it finds the slow rot every Node project accumulates: deprecated packages, functional duplicates nobody noticed they installed twice, packages a major version or more behind, oversized bundles, copyleft licenses hiding in a permissive project, and dependencies with no publish in two years. It rolls everything into a single 0–100 health score and tells you what to do about each finding.

articles.body: GTA 6's world won't be blocked off by story progression, Rockstar confirms. In a new preview from Edge magazine (as relayed by the podcast GTA VI O'Clock ), Rockstar Games confirmed a ton of new details about GTA 6. One of the big bits revealed was that GTA 6's map will open up relatively early. In some GTA games, like GTA 4, the game forces you to progress through its story before you can access the entire map. GTA 4's Liberty City uses police blockades on bridges to make sure the world only expands as Niko continues his journey. That changed in GTA 5, as you could go wherever your heart desired once the game's tutorials were finished. It seems like GTA 6 will be similar, as Edge's story confirms that the state of Leonida will open up relatively early on.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.body: Credit: NASA The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.   “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks for the ceremony. “NASA and the Vietnam National Space Center have built momentum in satellite innovation, land-use research, and radar-based Earth observation. Joining the Artemis Accords opens a new chapter in that relationship. We’ve aligned on the principles. The opportunities are in front of us, and now we can build on that foundation together.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).
